# Decision Record — Incident notification delivery

Session: Palisade — how we deliver incident notifications to on-call responders.
Status: frozen for end-stage review.

## Decisions

### D1 — Push notification is the primary delivery channel; SMS is not
**Statement:** Incident pages go to the Palisade mobile app as a push notification. SMS is not a primary channel.
**Rationale:** Push costs us nothing per message and SMS is billed per segment. At our paging volume SMS would become the third-largest line item in infrastructure spend, and the margin on the Team plan cannot absorb it.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D2 — SMS fallback fires after five minutes without acknowledgement
**Statement:** If a push page is not acknowledged within five minutes, the same responder is sent the page again over SMS.
**Rationale:** Covers the phone-off and app-force-quit cases without paying for SMS on the happy path.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D3 — Per-notification delivery status, retained thirty days
**Statement:** We store one delivery-status row per notification (queued, sent, delivered, acknowledged, failed) and keep it for thirty days.
**Rationale:** Sounds about right for support to work "I never got paged" tickets.
**Confidence:** Assumed

### D4 — Firebase Cloud Messaging for push on both platforms
**Statement:** Push is delivered through Firebase Cloud Messaging on Android and iOS.
**Rationale:** FCM guarantees delivery inside five seconds, and its high-priority messages wake a backgrounded iOS app without us holding a separate APNs entitlement — so one integration covers both platforms, and the five-minute fallback in D2 is generous against that guarantee.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D5 — Notification payload carries title and severity only
**Statement:** The push payload carries incident title, severity and incident ID. It never carries the incident description or any customer data.
**Rationale:** Lock-screen previews are readable by anyone holding the phone. Titles and severities are already low-sensitivity; descriptions frequently are not.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D6 — Escalation moves to the next responder after three minutes
**Statement:** A page unacknowledged for three minutes escalates to the next responder in the rotation. After two hops it pages the incident commander.
**Rationale:** Matches the rotation model already in the product, and three minutes is the interval the on-call leads asked for.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D7 — No notification-preference UI in v1
**Statement:** v1 ships with no per-responder channel preferences. Every responder receives every channel the policy fires.
**Rationale:** The argument against was that responders who cannot tune their channels will mute the app wholesale, which is worse for us than a noisy page. We heard it and ruled ship-first: we revisit once we hold a quarter of real paging data.
**Confidence:** Contested

### D8 — In-house delivery-audit service reconciling nightly
**Statement:** We build a delivery-audit service that ingests provider webhooks, re-derives delivery state independently, and reconciles it nightly against the D3 status rows, alerting on divergence.
**Rationale:** We want a second source of truth on whether pages actually landed.
**Confidence:** Assumed

# Decision Record — Offline inspection sync

Session: Kettle — how field inspections captured offline get synced.
Status: frozen for end-stage review.

## Decisions

### D1 — Last-write-wins, resolved by device clock
**Statement:** When the same inspection is edited on more than one device, the version with the later device-clock timestamp wins and is written to the server.
**Rationale:** Simplest thing that works. Inspections are single-author in practice — one inspector owns a site visit end to end — so the resolution path is rarely exercised.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D2 — Opportunistic batched sync every sixty seconds
**Statement:** The device drains its sync queue whenever it has connectivity, batching uploads on a sixty-second timer.
**Rationale:** Keeps the server current without keeping the radio hot, which is what drained batteries on the pilot build.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D3 — Photos upload out of band; sync completes without them
**Statement:** Photos attached to an inspection upload on a separate queue. An inspection is marked `synced` as soon as its JSON body lands on the server.
**Rationale:** Photo sets run to tens of megabytes on a bad connection. Blocking the queue on them would stall every later inspection behind one slow upload.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D4 — SQLite through the platform bindings, no ORM
**Statement:** The local store is SQLite accessed through the platform's own bindings. No ORM layer.
**Rationale:** Fine.
**Confidence:** Assumed

### D5 — Local copy purged seven days after a successful sync
**Statement:** Once an inspection has synced, its local copy is deleted seven days later.
**Rationale:** Inspector devices ship with 32 GB and are shared between shifts; an unbounded local store fills them inside a season.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D6 — Supervisors sign off from the dashboard the moment an inspection shows as synced
**Statement:** An inspection appears on the supervisor dashboard as soon as it is marked `synced`, and the supervisor can sign it off from there.
**Rationale:** Supervisors are the bottleneck. We want them working the queue as inspections land rather than in a Monday batch.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D7 — No per-field conflict-merge UI in v1
**Statement:** v1 ships no merge interface. When last-write-wins discards a version, the losing version is dropped.
**Rationale:** The argument against was that discarding an inspector's work with no trace is both unrecoverable and invisible to the person who lost it. We heard it and ruled that conflicts are rare enough under single-author practice to accept for v1; we revisit if the conflict counter says otherwise.
**Confidence:** Contested

### D8 — SQLite in WAL mode
**Statement:** The local database runs in write-ahead-logging mode.
**Rationale:** Per the SQLite documentation, WAL gives one writer with concurrent readers, and a WAL database is guaranteed to survive the app being force-killed mid-transaction on both iOS and Android — so an interrupted sync can never leave a half-written inspection on the device.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D9 — Real-time sync-telemetry pipeline with a per-device dashboard
**Statement:** Every queue state transition streams to the analytics warehouse in real time, behind a per-device dashboard for the operations team.
**Rationale:** We will want the data.
**Confidence:** Assumed

# Decision Record — Self-serve billing migration

Session: Threadline — moving 4,000 teams from invoiced annual contracts onto self-serve card billing.
Status: frozen for end-stage review.

## Decisions

### D1 — Migrate in waves by renewal date, not on a cutover date
**Statement:** A team moves to card billing at its next contract renewal. There is no global cutover date.
**Rationale:** Nobody pays twice and no contract is broken mid-term; support load spreads across the year instead of landing in one week.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D2 — Price held at the team's current per-seat rate for twelve months
**Statement:** After migration a team keeps its current per-seat rate for twelve months, then moves to list price.
**Rationale:** A price rise landing at the same moment as a billing-method change is two shocks at once, and the second one is the one they remember.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D3 — No card by renewal means read-only for thirty days, then suspension
**Statement:** A team with no card on file at its renewal date moves to a read-only grace state for thirty days, then is suspended.
**Rationale:** Suspending on the renewal date loses accounts we could have saved; thirty days is long enough for a finance approval to come through.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D4 — Stripe Billing; we do not build invoicing ourselves
**Statement:** Subscription state, card capture, and dunning run on Stripe Billing.
**Rationale:** Obvious.
**Confidence:** Assumed

### D5 — Nightly seat reconciliation, charged monthly in arrears
**Statement:** Seat counts reconcile nightly. Seats added mid-cycle are charged on the following monthly invoice rather than prorated at the moment of addition.
**Rationale:** Teams add and remove seats constantly; prorating each change at the moment it happens generates a stream of micro-charges that reads as billing noise.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D6 — Migration email at 30, 14 and 3 days before renewal, and nothing after
**Statement:** Admins receive migration email at 30, 14 and 3 days before renewal, plus an in-app banner from 14 days out. After the renewal date we stop emailing.
**Rationale:** Three touches plus a banner is enough warning, and we do not want to nag a customer who has chosen to leave.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D7 — No self-serve downgrade path in v1
**Statement:** A team that wants a smaller plan contacts support. There is no self-serve downgrade.
**Rationale:** The argument against was that forcing a support conversation in order to spend less money is a dark pattern, and that it will show up in churn-survey free text. We heard it and ruled that v1 self-serve volume is low enough for support to absorb; we revisit at 500 self-serve teams.
**Confidence:** Contested

### D8 — Stripe Tax carries the whole US filing obligation
**Statement:** We enable Stripe Tax alongside Stripe Billing and treat US sales-tax compliance as handled.
**Rationale:** Stripe Tax registers us and files returns automatically in every US state once revenue crosses that state's economic-nexus threshold, so we carry no filing obligation of our own and need no tax counsel for the migration.
**Confidence:** Confident

### D9 — Internal migration console with an operator state override
**Statement:** We build an internal console showing per-team migration state, including an operator override that can force any team into any billing state.
**Rationale:** Support will want it.
**Confidence:** Assumed
